title: Praedestinatus Sive Praedestinatorum Haeresis
author: Anonymus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp869.tmp869.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Prima et vicesima hæresis a Marcione orta est. Duo principia fuisse confirmat, boni et mali. Quem Eriphanius tria dicehat principia docuisse, boni, justi et pravi; sed Eusebius d Syrinum quemdam, no!! Marcionem, trium principiorum atque naturarum scribit auctorem. e Marcionitæ, cum universalem Orien- Lis Ecclesiam macularent, ab Origene superati, confutati, et per singulas sunt civitates damnati. Item post aliquantos annos, jam devicti atque delecti, in Africanis partibus pullulabant, quos Tertullianus modis omnibus ita obtinuit, ut ipsos faceret contra sectam suam publice prædicare.
passages.english: The twenty-first heresy arose from Marcion. He maintains that there were two principles, of good and of evil. Epiphanius said that he taught three principles, of the good, the just and the wicked; but Eusebius writes that a certain Syrinus, not Marcion, was the author of the three principles and natures. The Marcionites, when they were defiling the universal Church of the East, were overcome and refuted by Origen, and were condemned city by city. Likewise, after some years, though already defeated and destroyed, they were sprouting up again in the regions of Africa; Tertullian so prevailed over them by every means that he made them preach publicly against their own sect.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Eriphanius' read as Epiphanius, 'dicehat' as dicebat, 'no!!' as non, 'Orien- Lis' as Orientalis; stray letters 'd' and 'e' omitted as footnote marks. 'delecti' taken as 'deleti' (destroyed). 'Syrinum' (Syrinus) is unidentified; possibly a corruption of another name (e.g. Cerdo or a Syrian).

passages.original: De infantis sanguine eos accipere, quod ideo dicimus, ne videamur ignorare omnia quæ de eis dicuntur : hi enim qui contra eos scripserunt nibil hinc penitus memorarunt. d Scripsit contra eos libruni sanctus Soter papa Urbis, et Apol- lonius Ephesiorum antistes. Contra quos scripsit Tertullianus presbyter Carthaginiensis. Qui cum omnia bene et prime et incomparabiliter scripserit, in hoc solum se reprebensibilem fecit, quod Monlanum defendit, agens contra Soterem supra dictum Urbis papam, asserens falsa esse de sanguine infantis, Trinitatem in unitate Deilatis, pœnitentiam lapsis, mysteriis eisdem unum pascha nobiscum.
passages.english: [They say] that they receive [communion] from the blood of an infant; we mention this so that we may not seem to be ignorant of all that is said about them, for those who wrote against them recorded nothing at all on this point. The holy Soter, pope of the City, wrote a book against them, and so did Apollonius, bishop of the Ephesians. Against these Tertullian, a presbyter of Carthage, wrote. Though he wrote everything well, excellently and incomparably, in this alone he made himself blameworthy, that he defended Montanus, acting against the aforesaid Soter, pope of the City, and asserting that the [reports] about the blood of an infant are false, [and that they hold] the Trinity in the unity of the Godhead, penance for the lapsed, [and] with the same mysteries one Easter with us.
passages.notes: The last clause is compressed and its construction uncertain; it seems to list orthodox positions Tertullian claimed the Montanists held. The stray 'd' is a footnote mark; 'nibil', 'libruni', 'Monlanum', 'Deilatis' are scanning errors for nihil, librum, Montanum, Deitatis.

passages.original: Quid Bardesan dicitur perfectus fuisse catholicus, sed postea in id per Valentiui discipulum incurrisse, ut malam diceret carnis humanae creaturam, animae bonam. Hunc in Cappadocia damnavit Theocritus episcopus, docens Deum bonum utraque fecisse, utraque copulasse, et carnis humanae non naturam, sed prævaricationem esse culpandam.
passages.english: This Bardesanes is said to have been a perfect catholic, but afterwards, through a disciple of Valentinus, to have fallen into saying that the creation of human flesh was evil and that of the soul good. Bishop Theocritus condemned him in Cappadocia, teaching that the good God made both, joined both, and that what is to be blamed is not the nature of human flesh but its transgression.
passages.notes: 'Quid' is probably a scanning error for 'Qui' or 'Hic'. Theocritus is not otherwise identified.

passages.original: Tricesima octava hæresis est Catharorum, qui scipsos isto nomine quasi propter munditiam superbissime appellarunt. Secundas nuptias non admittunt. Pœnitentiam denegant, Novatum sectantes hæreticum: unde etiam Novatiani appellantur. Contra hunc beatus Xystus martyr rt episcopus, et venerabilis Cyprianus martyr Christi, tunc Carthaginiensis pontifex, scripsit contra Novalum librum deLapsis, quod possint per pœnitentiam recuperare gratiam quam labendo perdiderant, quod Novatus asserebat fleri omnino non posse.
passages.english: The thirty-eighth heresy is that of the Cathars, who most arrogantly called themselves by this name as if on account of their purity. They do not admit second marriages. They deny penance, following the heretic Novatus; hence they are also called Novatians. Against him the blessed Xystus, martyr and bishop, and the venerable Cyprian, martyr of Christ, then bishop of Carthage, [wrote]; [Cyprian] wrote against Novatus the book On the Lapsed, [arguing] that they can recover through penance the grace which they had lost by lapsing, which Novatus asserted could not happen at all.
passages.notes: The sentence is syntactically awkward (Xystus and Cyprian with singular 'scripsit'); rendered by sense.

passages.original: Quadragesima octava hæresis est Meletianorum, a Meletio quodam. Nolentes orare cum bis qui in per- secutione ceciderant, schisma fecerunt. Quibus restitit sanctus Basilius episcopus Cappadociae, dicens majorem spei et fidei charitatem quae omnia tolerat, et manum lapsis magis porrigendam. Hortatur etiam desperantes recoperatione provocandos ut redeant : siquidem etiam angelis in cœlo gaudium majus faciat unus poenitens, quam nonagiuta novem qui non peccaverunt ( Luc.
passages.english: The forty-eighth heresy is that of the Meletians, from a certain Meletius. Refusing to pray with those who had fallen in persecution, they made a schism. Saint Basil, bishop of Cappadocia, opposed them, saying that charity, which bears all things, is greater than hope and faith, and that a hand should rather be held out to the lapsed. He also urges that those who despair should be encouraged by [the prospect of] recovery to return, since even for the angels in heaven one penitent makes greater joy than ninety-nine who have not sinned (Luke
passages.notes: 'majorem spei et fidei charitatem' read as 'charity greater than hope and faith'. The reference continues in the following text (15:7).

passages.original: Denique in ipsa authentica hebdomada Paschæ, inventi sunt epulantes et porcorum carnibus trahentes convivia : ita ut assum porcum quem in mensa eorum invenerant, populi collo ejus suspenderent, et ita eum per totam civitatem facerent circuire. Scripsit etiam contra hos Hieronymus presbyter certos libros; quos qui plenius legerit, et quanta bona virginitas et continentia et abslinentia habeat discit, et quanta mala edacitas et luxuria habeat perhorrescit.
passages.english: Finally, in the very Holy Week of Easter they were found feasting and holding banquets of pork, so that the people hung a roast pig, which they had found on their table, around the neck of [one of them] and so made him go around the whole city. The presbyter Jerome also wrote certain books against them; whoever reads them more fully learns both how many good things virginity, continence and abstinence have, and shudders at how many evils gluttony and luxury have.
passages.notes: 'collo ejus' is ambiguous as to whose neck; perhaps Jovinian's.

passages.original: Octogesimam et tertiam hæresim in sexto libro historiograpbus noster ponit Eusebius, quam nec Epiphanius alicubi memoravit, nec Polycrates, nec Africanus, nec Hesiodus, qui Graeco sermone univer- sas hæreses describentes volumina multorum condidere librorum. In sexto itaque, ut dixi, libro narrat Eusebius esse in Arabia hæreticos, quorum quia auctorem non memorat, nos possumus eos nuncupare Arabicos. Hi, inquit, dicunt animas cum corporibus mori atque dissolvi, et in line sæculi utrumque repa- rari. Sed hos disputatione Origenis magna memorat ex parte revocatos.
passages.english: Our historian Eusebius places the eighty-third heresy in his sixth book, one which neither Epiphanius mentioned anywhere, nor Polycrates, nor Africanus, nor Hesiod, who, describing all heresies in the Greek language, composed volumes of many books. So in the sixth book, as I said, Eusebius relates that there are heretics in Arabia; since he does not mention their founder, we may call them Arabici. These, he says, say that souls die and are dissolved with their bodies, and that at the end of the age both are restored. But he records that they were in large part brought back by the disputation of Origen.
passages.notes: 'Hesiodus' as a heresiologist is unidentified and probably an error of the author or text.

passages.original: eam dicant de Joseph post nativitatem Christi alios filios peperisse. Isti quidem nuper. id est sub Siricio Romanorum antistite orti sunt, et per Italiam atque Gallias direxerunt suos discipulos. Contra hos scripsit Hieronymus doctor egregius b duos libros, quos lectos in tempore digna eos exsecratione c anathematizabant. Epiphanius autem noster, scrutator hærelicorum, scribens contra hos libellum, qui in illo tempore hanc blasphemiis plenam assertionem proferebant.
passages.english: [...] that she bore other children by Joseph after the birth of Christ. These indeed arose recently, that is under Siricius, bishop of the Romans, and sent their disciples throughout Italy and Gaul. Against them the outstanding doctor Jerome wrote two books; when these were read at the time, they anathematized them with fitting execration. And our Epiphanius, investigator of heretics, writing a pamphlet against those who at that time were putting forward this assertion full of blasphemies,
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence ('eam' likely for 'ut eam'). The final sentence is completed in the following context ('decided they should be called Antidicomarians'). Stray 'b', 'c' are footnote marks. Jerome is credited with two books; the subject of 'anathematizabant' is unstated.

passages.original: Hic cum se presbyterum diceret Tertullianistam, meruit per sacrum scriptum ut sibi collegium extra muros Urbis fabricaret. Quod dum impetrasset a tyranno Maximo, sanctorum nostrorum exclusit locum, id est duorum fratrum Processi et Martiniani, dicens eos Phryges fuisse, et ideo hanc legem tenuisse, quam Tertullianus : atque hoc ordine per occasionem martyrum Dei populum seducebat. Deo autem Theodosio religioso Augusto dante victoriam, punitoque satellite Maximi de cujus se Tertullianista potestate jactabat, statim fugit cum matrona quæ venerat, nec viventis nec mortui rumore rcnovato.
passages.english: When this man called himself a Tertullianist presbyter, he obtained by a sacred rescript [permission] to build himself a meeting-house outside the walls of the City. Having obtained this from the usurper Maximus, he shut out the shrine of our saints, that is, of the two brothers Processus and Martinian, saying that they had been Phrygians and had therefore held the same rule as Tertullian; and in this way, using the martyrs as a pretext, he was leading God's people astray. But when God gave victory to the religious Augustus Theodosius, and the henchman of Maximus, of whose power the Tertullianist boasted, had been punished, he immediately fled with the matron who had come, and no report of him, living or dead, was heard again.
passages.notes: 'sanctorum nostrorum exclusit locum' could mean he took over or excluded [us from] the shrine; sense uncertain.

passages.original: Octogesimam et octavam hæresim in Pelagio se invenisse sedes apostolica sub papa sancto Innocentio docuit, dum Coclestius Pelagii discipulus apud Carthaginem doceret posse homines sine peccato esse, natura sibi sufficiente sola humana. Restitit ei quidam Paulinus diaconus, defensor et procurator ecclesiae Mediolanensis : cuique in conventu sacerdotum multa capitula objecit contra fidem catholicam, quæ Coelestius damnare neglexit, dicens : Non ad me pertinet de his quæ objecit, ubi meum nomen est, et crimen alienum.
passages.english: The apostolic see under the holy Pope Innocent taught that it had found the eighty-eighth heresy in Pelagius, when Caelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, was teaching at Carthage that men can be without sin, human nature alone being sufficient for them. A certain Paulinus, a deacon, defender and procurator of the church of Milan, opposed him, and in an assembly of bishops raised against him many articles contrary to the catholic faith, which Caelestius neglected to condemn, saying: "What he has raised does not concern me, where my name is attached but the offence is another's."
passages.notes: 'Coclestius' read as Caelestius. The sense of Caelestius' reply is somewhat uncertain.

passages.original: llli autem, sive antequam damnarentur ab universali Ecclesia, sive posteaquam damnati sunt, non cessaverunt scribere posse hominem sine peccato esse, et nihil obfuisse Adam generi humano, et legem sic misisse ad regnum sicut Evangelia, ct infantes non ideo baptizandos, quia habere possint originale peccatum; et naturam tam bene factam a Deo, ut sibi sola sufficiat ad hoc ut possit carere peccato. Contra hos suscepit sine scriptura quidam Constantius tractator. Post hunc autem, scripsit contra hos et Augustinus Hipponensis episcopus et Hieronymus presbyter a Bethleites. Pelagiani tamen seu Coelestiani, catholicæ plebi permixti sunt, quia eo clesiam aliam non habent: et ideo ubi eis evenerit, communionem non renuunt.
passages.english: But they, whether before they were condemned by the universal Church or after they were condemned, did not cease to write that man can be without sin, that Adam did no harm to the human race, that the Law sent [men] to the kingdom just as the Gospels do, that infants are not to be baptized on the ground that they could have original sin, and that nature was made so well by God that it alone suffices for itself to be able to be free of sin. Against them a certain Constantius, a preacher, took [them] on without writing. After him Augustine, bishop of Hippo, and Jerome, presbyter of Bethlehem, wrote against them. The Pelagians or Caelestians, however, are mingled with the catholic people, because they have no other church; and so, wherever it happens to them, they do not refuse communion.
passages.notes: 'eo clesiam' read as 'ecclesiam'; 'a Bethleites' as 'Bethlehemites'. 'sine scriptura' (without writing) is odd; perhaps orally, or text corrupt.

passages.original: Finitus est libcr b inimicus hominum, contra fidem catholicam confictus ; liber dolosus, circumdatus fallaciis, adulter integræ definitionis ; quique, ut sanctus Cyprianus ait, falsa ostentat ut vera subripiat. Qui sub specie pietatis editus, agit contra omnium instituta sanctorum. Hujus libri causa, ut memoravimus in præfatiuncula, omnium hæreticorum in unum librum collegimus sectas, ut sciant defensores ejus cunctis nos hæresibus adversari;
passages.english: [Here] ends the book, enemy of men, fabricated against the catholic faith; a deceitful book, wrapped in fallacies, adulterer of sound definition; one which, as Saint Cyprian says, displays false things in order to steal away true ones. Issued under the appearance of piety, it acts against the teachings of all the saints. Because of this book, as we mentioned in the little preface, we have collected the sects of all heretics into one book, so that its defenders may know that we oppose all heresies;
passages.notes: Stray 'b' after 'liber' omitted as a footnote mark.

passages.original: Qui metius a Christo sapitis, dicile si mentitus est Christus, et ita demum asserite nos contra Christi regulam istam b fixisse sententiam. Si enim verum dixit Christus, non mentimur quod dicimus prædestinatos trahi ad vitam, quia vita ipse eat. c Non est novum vocis sono decipi posse stultos. Sic vanus Arius, secutus vocis sonum, dicit Filio Patrem ejus esse majorem. Et hoc dicit nobis, quod dicitis vos : Si ipsi Filio creditis, ipsum audite. Dicit enim quia Pater major me est (Joan. xiv, 28). Vocis sonum qui attendit, sicut Arianorum hæresi, sic Praedestinatorum vanitati conjungitur.
passages.english: You who think you are wiser than Christ, say whether Christ lied, and only then assert that we have fixed this opinion contrary to that rule of Christ. For if Christ spoke the truth, we do not lie when we say that the predestined are drawn to life, since he himself is life. It is nothing new that fools can be deceived by the sound of a word. So the empty Arius, following the sound of a word, says that the Father is greater than his Son. And he says to us what you say: "If you believe the Son himself, listen to him. For he says: The Father is greater than I (John 14:28)." Whoever attends to the sound of a word is joined to the vanity of the Predestinarians just as to the heresy of the Arians.
passages.notes: 'metius' read as melius; 'dicile' as dicite; 'eat' as est; stray letters 'b', 'c' omitted.

passages.original: Si ergo antequam vera et integra liberlas nostra veniret, Dominus Jesus Christus, a justus voluntarie sactificavit Deo, et ex voluntate sua confessus est, peccator ex voluntate deliquit; quanto magis nunc, instaurata npbis libertate per Christum, universa nostro jure sunt reddita, non natura dominante, ut Pelagius et Cœlestius definivit, non natura hominis dominante, sed Christi gratia condonante? Non suis viribus imputando, sed de Dei adminiculis præsumendo ; non sibi aliquid usurpando, sed totum Dci gratiæ imputando?
passages.english: If, therefore, before our true and complete liberty, the Lord Jesus Christ, came, the just man voluntarily sacrificed to God and confessed by his own will, [and] the sinner transgressed by his own will, how much more now, when our liberty has been restored to us through Christ, have all things been given back to our own right, not with nature ruling, as Pelagius and Caelestius defined, not with man's nature ruling, but with the grace of Christ bestowing [it]? Not by ascribing [anything] to one's own powers, but by relying on God's aids; not by claiming anything for oneself, but by ascribing the whole to the grace of God?
passages.notes: Syntax of the first sentence is awkward; 'Dominus Jesus Christus' may be misplaced or corrupt (perhaps it belongs with 'veniret', i.e. 'before the Lord Jesus Christ, our true liberty, came'). Scanning errors 'liberlas', 'sactificavit', 'npbis', 'Dci' corrected; stray 'a' omitted.
